title: The spring equinox
hook: day and night equal: an image of balance

segments.voice: Yesterday: Janus in the doorway, one face back and one forward. Your line was both ways. Did a doorway remind you to look back once, then forward once? Day six hundred sixty-seven.

Twice a year, the sun, as seen from Earth, crosses the line of the equator, and for a day the whole planet, from Oslo to Cape Town, gets roughly the same amount of light and dark. Twelve hours, give or take. In March, for the northern half of the world, the light is winning from here on. Many peoples have marked it: Nowruz, the Persian new year, begins at that moment, and the date of Easter is still reckoned from a spring equinox fixed at March 21. Today, on the porch, we look at the spring equinox as a picture, and ask what it shows.
screen: `THE SUN CROSSES THE EQUATOR.` → `TWELVE HOURS, GIVE OR TAKE.` → `A PICTURE OF BALANCE.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Equinox comes from Latin, aequinoctium: equal night. And a small surprise: it isn't exactly equal. Because the sun is a disk, not a point, and the air bends its light, most places get a few minutes more day than night on the equinox itself. The truly equal day comes a little before it in spring. Balance in nature is close, not perfect. Second, the Stoic picture of balance. Seneca, writing to his friend Serenus about peace of mind, gives a list of alternations. Mix solitude and company: being alone makes us long for people, and people make us long to be alone, and each cures the other. Give the mind rest, he says, the way you'd let a field lie fallow, because ground forced to produce every year wears out. He mentions that Socrates wasn't ashamed to play with small children. Third, what that balance isn't. It isn't a perfect fifty-fifty schedule, like the equinox that's never quite exact. It's noticing which way you've tipped. Too much work, not enough rest. Too many people, not enough quiet. Too much screen, not enough sky. Fourth, why spring is a good time to check. Things are about to grow fast. Days lengthen. Plans multiply. Before the light runs away with you, the equinox stands still for a day and says: here is what even looks like. Now choose where to add a little light, and where to let a little dark stay.
screen: `AEQUINOCTIUM: EQUAL NIGHT, NEARLY.` · `SOLITUDE AND COMPANY, WORK AND REST.` · `NOTICE WHICH WAY YOU'VE TIPPED.` · `CHECK BEFORE THE LIGHT RUNS AWAY.` · then, large: `EQUAL LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Picture your ordinary day as a scale. On one side, everything that fills it: work, errands, screens, people. On the other: rest, quiet, play, time outside. Which side hangs lower? Don't scold yourself; just see it. Now choose one small thing to move across. Ten minutes of quiet. One walk without your phone. One call to a friend if you've been alone too much. Picture the scale shifting, just slightly. The bell holds the time.
Aequinoctium, Latin for equal night, the root of the word equinox, when day and night come close to even. Today's word.
Your line: equal light. Move the one small thing you chose across the scale today, and notice how the day feels with it there. Day six hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: Many cultures mark the spring equinox with new-year or spring festivals; some people use it as a moment to look at the balance of work, rest and company in their lives.

myth: on the equinox, day and night are exactly twelve hours everywhere
most places get a few minutes more day; the sun is a disk and the air bends light.
Seneca advised mixing solitude with company
being alone makes us long for people, and people make us long to be alone.
Seneca thought the mind should work without rest
he compared a rested mind to a field left fallow.

fork.setup: you've worked straight through for weeks and feel worn down. what does Seneca recommend?
options: push harder until the work is done
give the mind rest, like a fallow field
fork.reveal: in On Tranquility of Mind he says ground forced to produce without a break wears out; the mind needs rest too.

original.note: Latin: equal night, the root of equinox.

trapdoor: what you thought: the equinox is when day and night are perfectly equal.
what it means: they're nearly equal, a picture of balance that's close rather than exact.
what a scholar hears: aequus, equal, plus nox, night; the day of truly equal light, sometimes called the equilux, falls a few days before the spring equinox.

sources.work: Seneca, On Tranquility of Mind (De Tranquillitate Animi)

notes: On Tranquility of Mind 17 paraphrased (alternate solitude and crowds; mind must be given rest like fertile fields; Socrates not ashamed to play with children). Confirm section number and details.
Equinox astronomy: day slightly longer than night because of the sun's angular size and atmospheric refraction; equilux a few days before the March equinox in the northern hemisphere. Confirm.
Nowruz begins at the moment of the March equinox (vernal for the northern hemisphere). Confirm. Other spring festivals mentioned only generally.
Seasons are for the northern hemisphere; southern-hemisphere listeners have autumn in March. Consider a line acknowledging this.

Audit (year 2, second sample): the hook's vague claim that 'several calendars of spring festivals are counted from it' was replaced with a checkable one (Easter's date is reckoned from an equinox fixed at March 21); confirm wording covers both Western and Orthodox reckoning (Orthodox use March 21 on the Julian calendar).
